newsitem.title: LEBANON: Chirac ends tour as Arab hero, bogeyman in Israel.
newsitem.headline: Chirac ends tour as Arab hero, bogeyman in Israel.

text.p: The Arab world has a new hero, the Israeli right a new bogeyman: French President Jacques Chirac.

His tumultuous week-long Middle East tour has made him the most popular European leader in Arab countries since his mentor, General Charles De Gaulle, imposed an arms embargo on Israel after the 1967 Middle East war.
A Palestinian woman in Gaza even named her newly-born baby "Jacques Chirac Jibril" in his honour.

Chirac used all the power of French rhetoric to plead for a Palestinian state, the return of occupied Arab land to Syria and Lebanon, an easing of the economic stranglehold on Iraq and a new understanding between Islam and the West.
He also declared himself a friend of Israel, urged acceptance of its security needs and denied as "absurd" any intention of competing with the United States as a mediator.

But it remains uncertain whether Chirac achieved his stated goal of increasing Europe's political role in Arab-Israeli peace negotiations, turning the main paymaster of the peace process into a co-sponsor alongside the United States and Russia.

Not all the 15 European Union states seem to want such an active role. Britain and Germany, keen to avoid crossing Washington or Israel, have doubts. Some smaller EU states care more about human rights and development than power-broking.
Chirac's dramatic confrontation with heavy-handed Israeli security men who "protected" him from contact with Palestinians in Jerusalem's Old City won plaudits from Amman to Rabat.
Enthusiastic mass welcomes in Damascus, the West Bank town of Ramallah and Gaza were strong symbols of the rebirth of France's "Arab policy".

Egypt's al-Akhbar newspaper called him a "valiant knight". Beirut's French-language l'Orient-le Jour hailed him as a "messenger of peace, champion of just causes and even, for millions of Arabs, a true hero out of some tale of mediaeval chivalry."

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu apologised for the Old City incident and, while rebuffing any EU role in peace negotiations, said he would welcome French help to improve Israel's relations with its Arab neighbours.
Yet the mixture of right-wing hostility and public indifference to Chirac's visit indicated how little faith the Israelis have in his even-handedness.

At each stop on his tour of Syria, Israel, the Palestinian territories, Jordan and Lebanon, the French president hammered home his message that the U.S.-led peace process was in crisis due to a lack of confidence and an Arab perception of imbalance, which Europe could help rectify.
But the international Arabic-language daily al-Hayat asked the same question as the Israeli media: Could such a friend of the Arabs be accepted as an honest broker by the Jewish state?

"Chirac tried to play it smart and chose a most critical time, when the U.S. administration is busy with presidential elections, to try to push for a French or European role in the peace process, but Israel's rough reaction and hostile reception shattered his hope for such a role," it said.
His trip may boost France's commercial interests in the Arab world, as well as its political standing. But it raised expectations across the region which may be hard to follow up.

The next step depends partly on whether France can persuade the EU to appoint a permanent Middle East peace envoy, rather than just sending an ever-changing troika of foreign ministers on multilingual fact-finding missions.
It may also hinge on whether Arab leaders use France or the EU as a vehicle for making small gestures towards the Israelis which they have denied to the United States.
They did so in April when French Foreign Minister Herve De Charette helped broker a ceasefire between Israel and Lebanese Hizbollah guerrillas in southern Lebanon.
Syrian President Hafez al-Assad sent a positive message to Netanyahu via Chirac, French and Israeli officials said.

A senior French official said Assad hinted he was willing to go further than in previous negotiations on security measures to satisfy the Israelis on the Golan Heights, provided there was a clear understanding they would be returned to Syria.

He could enhance France's role by helping return missing Israeli airman Ron Arad, shot down over Lebanon in 1986, or by agreeing to extradite wanted Nazi war criminal Alois Brunner, whom French justice authorities believe is in Syria.

Despite his call for a French role in the talks, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat appeared to use Chirac more as a wailing wall to pour out his grievances against the Netanyahu government than as a conduit for substantive negotiation.
It remains to be seen whether the man whom Arafat called "doctor Chirac" will be able to fulfil the hopes he has raised.
